transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you so much for seeing me. I really appreciate it. Um, I hope I'm not taking up too much of your time with this. It's probably just a small thing, really, but... well, what finally pushed me to come in is that I've been having some trouble at work. 

I manage a clinic, and I'll sit down to do an EPIC quality report, or I'll be in one of our clinic metrics meetings, and I have every intention of tracking it—I really do try my best to stay engaged. But within just a few minutes, my mind just sort of... drifts off? And then I'm sitting there rereading the same numbers over and over, or I suddenly realize I completely missed the whole point of the discussion. 

It's a little embarrassing to admit, honestly, because I really care about my job. Am I explaining that okay? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.
Would you say you've had this kind of trouble focusing your whole life, even back in school, or is this something new that's started more recently?

Um, well... I suppose it's not entirely new? I mean, I really don't want to make it sound like I was a terrible student or anything, because I always wanted to do well and please my teachers. 

But, um... even back in elementary school, I remember my teachers writing on my report cards that I was bright—which was very kind of them to say—but they would usually add that I was a little, um, careless. I always felt so bad about that word, because I really wasn't trying to be careless! My mother actually used to have to sit right there with me at the kitchen table while I finished my homework. Not because I couldn't understand the material, but mostly just because I would... you know, lose track of what the actual assignments were, or I'd accidentally forget to bring my books home from school. 

Is that the kind of thing you're asking about? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right background.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed a persistent low mood or a loss of interest or pleasure in things you normally enjoy?

Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I still really enjoy my life and my family. I love gardening on the weekends, and I still look forward to that just as much as I always have. 

I don't think I've felt down or anything like that. I really try to stay positive! It's just... this frustration with my focus at work that's been bothering me. But my mood itself has been perfectly fine, I promise. Does that make sense? I hope I'm answering that clearly enough.
Do you notice yourself worrying excessively about various things—like work, family, or health—more days than not, even when there's no clear reason to worry?

Oh, um, no, not really. I mean, I care about my family and my job, of course—I always want to make sure I'm doing a good job and that everyone is happy and taken care of. But I wouldn't say I worry *excessively*, or for no reason. 

I try not to be a worrier, honestly. I think I handle stress pretty well, all things considered. It's really just the... the drifting off during meetings and reports that's been the issue. I'm not sitting there feeling anxious or anything like that. I hope that's the right answer? I just don't want to give you the impression that I'm, you know, overly anxious or anything.
Do you often feel excessively sleepy or have trouble staying awake during the day, even after a full night's sleep?

Oh, no, definitely not. I mean, working in health services management, the days can be quite full, so I might feel a normal amount of tired by the time I get home, just like anyone else. But I'm certainly not falling asleep at my desk or having trouble staying awake during the day! 

I always make it a point to get a good night's rest so I can be fully present for my team. I really wouldn't want you to think I'm, you know, dozing off on the job or lacking energy or anything like that. I'm usually very awake and ready to go. Is that what you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.
Do you often find yourself feeling restless, fidgeting, or having trouble sitting still, or do you tend to interrupt others or act impulsively?

Oh, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, I'm pretty good at sitting through long meetings—it comes with the territory in management, right? I don't think I'm fidgety or restless. And I always try to be very respectful of others when they're speaking, so I definitely try my hardest not to interrupt. 

Sometimes I might get a little eager to share an idea if I think it'll help the team, but I wouldn't call it impulsive. I really try to be professional and polite. I hope that makes sense? I just wouldn't want you to think I'm running around the office or talking over people, because I really do try to be a good listener. Did I answer that okay?

Aside from work, do you notice similar difficulties—like losing track of things, forgetting tasks, or getting easily distracted—in other areas of your life, such as at home or when managing personal errands?

Well, at home, I really try my best to keep everything running smoothly. I definitely don't want my family to feel like I'm disorganized, so I put a lot of effort into that! But, um... I guess outside of my actual job, I do help out with some volunteer health workshops. Or, well, I did. I actually had to step back from leading parts of them recently. I just... I found that I couldn't reliably keep all the planning pieces moving, and I really, really didn't want to let the community or the other volunteers down. I hope it was the right decision to step back? I just thought it was best for the program.

And, honestly, if I'm being completely open with you... it has been spilling over at the clinic a little bit, too. My delays have started affecting our clinic reporting deadlines, which means... well, I'm making other teams wait on me. It's incredibly embarrassing to admit that out loud, because I really pride myself on being a supportive manager. I hate being the bottleneck. I just want to do a good job for everyone, you know? 

Does that answer what you were asking? I hope you don't think I'm completely dropping the ball everywhere... I really am trying my hardest to keep it all together.

Thinking back to before you turned 12, did your inattentiveness—like losing track of assignments or forgetting things—cause noticeable problems in more than one setting, such as both at school and at home?

Oh, well... I was always a very well-behaved kid, I promise. I really wanted to please my teachers and do a good job. But, um... yes, I suppose there were some little hiccups back then, too, both at school and at home. 

Even in elementary school, I remember my teachers writing on my report cards that I was bright, but... maybe just a little careless. I really didn't mean to be! And at home, my mother actually had to sit with me while I finished my homework. It was mostly because I would, you know, lose track of my assignments or accidentally forget my books at school. 

I always felt so guilty making her take that extra time to sit with me, because I really wasn't trying to be difficult or anything. I just couldn't seem to keep it all straight in my head. Does that answer what you were asking? I hope I'm giving you the right kind of examples... I just wouldn't want you to think I was a bad student or a troublemaker, because I really did try my best!
